concepts.title: Mustachios as Class Badges
concepts.definition: Mulk Raj Anand uses two moustaches as comic emblems of social pretension: the upturned, fierce moustache of the old feudal landowner, once a badge of aristocracy, and the small, tooth-brush moustache of the nouveau riche moneylender -- the new commercial class aping gentility.
concepts.key_idea: Hairs on a lip become heraldry -- Anand's satire on class pride and its imitation.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww102.txt opening sections (upturned moustache of the landowner, tooth brush moustache of the moneylender, nouveau riche, blue blood)

solution_steps.explain: The eagle-tailed, upturned moustache is the hereditary emblem of the landed feudal chief.
The moneylender's stiff little brush moustache imitates the newest English fashion of the commercial class.
By reducing class to facial hair, Anand mocks how superficial and hollow status symbols are.

concepts.title: The Quarrel over the Two Moustaches
concepts.definition: The moneylender flattens his moustache with pomade to mimic the new style, enraging the old Khan, who demands he curl it up as tradition dictates. The quarrel escalates absurdly to insults and litigation talk, until the parody ends with everyone wearing their moustache exactly as fashion -- not birth -- decides.
concepts.key_idea: A war over waxed hair -- pride battles pride while fashion quietly wins the day.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww102.txt quarrel sections (pomade and flattening, the khan's rage, escalation of the quarrel, jewellery and talk of courts)

solution_steps.explain: The flattened moustache appears in the old man's presence, an insult his feudal pride cannot digest.
Insults fly over hair and heritage, with each side invoking ancestors and dignity for something wax and pomade control.
Fashion, not feudal decree, finally rules the moustaches -- a quiet defeat for both kinds of pride.

concepts.title: Satire on a Society in Transition
concepts.definition: Beneath the comedy lies a picture of India in transition: feudal landowners fading, commercial classes rising, and both clinging to badges instead of substance. Anand suggests that aristocracy of blood and pride of the parvenu are equally absurd when times are changing the social order beneath them.
concepts.key_idea: Old pride and new money are mirror fools -- the real story is a social order changing under their feet.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww102.txt social context (feudal order declining, commercial classes rising, social transition, satire on status symbols)

solution_steps.explain: The Khan's lineage and the moneylender's new wealth represent two orders crossing in history.
Both mistake symbols -- hair, jewels, titles -- for the substance of worth.
When society changes, pride based on badges becomes comedy; the story laughs both classes into perspective.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Trace the escalation of the quarrel between the Khan and the moneylender, stage by stage.

solution_template.explain: The moneylender wears his moustache flat in the English style before the old Khan.
The Khan demands traditional curling; the moneylender defies him, invoking the new age.
Threats, ancestral boasts and near-litigation follow, until the absurdity of fighting over hair defuses itself.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A student calls the story a trivial joke about moustaches. Argue that it carries serious social meaning.

solution_template.explain: On the surface it is pure farce about two hairy badges.
The moustaches stand for feudalism and the rising commercial class -- history in miniature.
The triviality is the technique: Anand makes class pretension look exactly as silly as it is.
